findings.claim: The exam starts from 1558, but Elizabeth's background is still useful context.
findings.truth: The option is 'Elizabethan England, c1568-1603' - the last 35 years of the reign. Elizabeth's background is named content inside Part one, but the examined period starts at c1568, not 1558.
findings.evidence: spec p30, option BC 'Elizabethan England, c1568-1603'

findings.claim: AQA has named the Spanish Armada as the historic environment for your 2027 exam. (same opening in Lesson 17 for Kenilworth)
findings.truth: The board must never be named in student-facing text. Say the site is the named historic environment for that year.
findings.evidence: house standing rule; same wording in L16 and L17

findings.claim: is a site-based cause with a consequence - Level 4 material.
findings.truth: 'Level 1' to 'Level 9' are banned band names. Use the house vocabulary: top band.

findings.claim: Treat them as you would any source in Section B
findings.truth: Section codes are house-banned. Say 'this section'.

findings.claim: Between 1588 and 1591, her four closest advisors - Cecil, Dudley, Walsingham, and Hatton - all died.
findings.truth: Only three died in that window: Dudley (4 Sep 1588), Walsingham (6 Apr 1590), Hatton (20 Nov 1591). William Cecil, Lord Burghley, died on 4 August 1598. Lessons 1 and 3 both say Cecil served Elizabeth for 40 years, which only works to 1598.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'William Cecil, 1st Baron Burghley'; internal contradiction with L1 and L3

findings.claim: Robert Devereux became the Earl of Essex aged just 7 when his father died.
findings.truth: He was born on 10 November 1565 and his father Walter Devereux died in September 1576, so he was 10.

findings.claim: executed on 25 February 1601 at the Tower of London - just two weeks after his trial
findings.truth: He was tried on 19 February 1601 and executed on 25 February 1601: six days.

findings.claim: Martin Luther nailed his 95 complaints to a cathedral door (repeated in knowledge check 3)
findings.truth: The Ninety-five Theses are traditionally said to have gone on the door of All Saints' Church (the Castle Church) in Wittenberg on 31 October 1517. It was a church, not a cathedral.

findings.claim: By 1558, the Reformation had caused violent conflict across Europe. In France, thousands of Protestants were killed in the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572.
findings.truth: A massacre of 1572 cannot be evidence for the state of Europe 'by 1558'. The date of the massacre is right; the framing is an anachronism.

findings.claim: Top-band model answer: 'The threat escalated in 1570 when the Pope excommunicated Elizabeth... This helped trigger plots and the Northern Rebellion.'
findings.truth: The Northern Rebellion ran in November 1569; Regnans in Excelsis was issued on 25 February 1570, partly in response to it. Lesson 6 states this correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Rising of the North' and 'Regnans in Excelsis'; internal contradiction with L6

findings.claim: Sir Christopher Hatton - Elizabeth's childhood friend who organised the Queen's progresses.
findings.truth: Hatton was born on 12 December 1540, seven years after Elizabeth, and first caught her attention dancing in a masque at the Inner Temple about 1561. Robert Dudley, not Hatton, was her childhood companion.

findings.claim: Northumberland was captured in 1572.
findings.truth: Thomas Percy fled to Scotland after the rising, was taken there in 1569, was sold to the English by the Earl of Morton in 1572 and beheaded at York on 22 August 1572.

findings.claim: In 1568, the Catholic Church set up a training college at Douai... It was run by the Jesuits... These Jesuit priests secretly stayed in the homes of wealthy Catholic families.
findings.truth: The English College at Douai was founded in 1568 by William Allen and was a seminary for secular priests. The Jesuit mission to England is a separate, later strand, beginning in 1580 with Campion and Persons.

findings.claim: 1571: Recusancy fines introduced for Catholics who did not attend Protestant services.
findings.truth: Recusancy fines began with the 1559 Act of Uniformity (one shilling), which Lesson 2 teaches correctly. The 1571 statutes made it treason to bring in papal bulls and banned Catholic objects; the 1581 Act raised the fine to GBP 20 a month.

findings.claim: Francis Throckmorton, a young Catholic nobleman
findings.truth: Throckmorton was a gentleman, the son of a judge, not a nobleman. Lesson 14 already calls Babington a gentleman.

findings.claim: Other MPs like Peter Wentworth and Thomas Cartwright also tried to pass reform laws.
findings.truth: Wentworth was an MP; Cartwright was never one. He was Lady Margaret Professor of Divinity at Cambridge and a Presbyterian preacher.

findings.claim: Some of Elizabeth's own senior figures were Puritan sympathisers, including the MP John Field...
findings.truth: John Field was a London lecturer, curate and schoolmaster - a preacher, never an MP and never in Elizabeth's government. He had friends on the Council, which is a different claim.

findings.claim: The magnetic compass measured east-west position.
findings.truth: A compass gives a bearing, not a position. Longitude could not be measured at sea in this period at all; the sentence teaches a physical impossibility.

findings.claim: In 1564, he captured a Spanish ship and sold the enslaved people on board for a huge profit.
findings.truth: Hawkins's first slaving voyage sailed in 1562; he seized about 300 people on the African coast around Sierra Leone and sold them in the Spanish Caribbean. 1564 was his second voyage, and no Spanish slave ship was taken.

findings.claim: The only clue was the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a tree
findings.truth: CROATOAN was cut into a post of the palisade near the entrance; only the letters 'CRO' were on a tree.

findings.claim: Henry VII's eldest son Arthur died weeks after marrying the Spanish princess, Catherine of Aragon.
findings.truth: They married on 14 November 1501; Arthur died on 2 April 1502 - about four and a half months.

findings.claim: The City of London banned theatres within the city walls - which is why they were built in Southwark.
findings.truth: They were pushed outside the walls generally: The Theatre (1576) and The Curtain stood in Shoreditch, north of the city; The Rose, Swan and Globe were in Southwark.

findings.claim: Auto-generated cloze cards are broken across every lesson: mangled answers with stripped punctuation ('Elizabeths', 'Marys', 'Spains', 'Drakes', 'Mercators', 'Bartholomews', '15681587', '15941597'), answers that are the first word of a heading ('Case', 'Context', 'Background', 'Problem', 'Refusal'), answers that appear inside their own question ('Catholic', 'Essex', 'Throckmorton', 'Spanish', 'Pamphlets'), questions opening on orphan pronouns, and duplicate answers within one deck (L2, L3, L11, L12).
findings.truth: 58 cards rebuilt as proper questions opening What/Which/Who/When/Name, each answer unique within its deck and absent from its own question. Lessons 16 and 17 already had clean hand-written decks.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_HISTORY.md validator limits; brief's flashcard checklist

findings.claim: Lesson 9 dates the Armada in New Style (sighted 29 July, fireships 6-7 August, Gravelines 8 August). Lesson 16 dates the same events in Old Style (sighted 19 July, anchorage 27 July, fireships 28 July, Gravelines 29 July).
findings.truth: Both are internally consistent; they cannot both stand in one unit. Option A: move Lesson 9 to Old Style, the convention in English GCSE texts and the style Lesson 16 already uses (ripple: 4 content date labels, the 4 left-hand items of knowledge check 5, 2 model answers). Option B: move Lesson 16 to New Style (ripple: 5 places). Recommend Option A.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Spanish Armada' (Old Style English dates); internal L9 vs L16 clash

findings.claim: Lesson 9: 'Only about 80 ships made it back to Spain' (also the conclusion, knowledge check 3 and two model answers). Lesson 16: 'Perhaps half the ships that left Spain never returned.'
findings.truth: Sources give 44 to 63 ships lost, so 67 to 86 returned; 130 minus the 63 losses cited for the Irish coast article gives 67. Knowledge check 3 offers 65 as a distractor and marks 80 correct, so a well-read student picking 65 is marked wrong. Recommend setting both lessons to 'about two-thirds returned' and moving the knowledge check key to 65.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Spanish Armada' and 'Spanish Armada in Ireland'

findings.claim: Essex 'went to court aged 17', 'At 26, he was made a Privy Councillor', 'At 29, he led a successful attack on... Cadiz' (the ages also key the left column of knowledge check 5 and one model answer).
findings.truth: The chain fits a birth of November 1566. The ODNB and Wikipedia give 10 November 1565, which makes him 19 at court (September 1585), 27 on the Privy Council (February 1593) and 30 at Cadiz (June 1596). F29 has fixed the plainly wrong 'aged just 7'. Recommend moving the whole chain to 19 / 27 / 30 for consistency with that birth date.

findings.claim: 'Parker expelled 30 ministers' (conclusion, knowledge check 5 right-hand column, and three model answers).
findings.truth: At Lambeth in March 1566, 61 London clergy subscribed and 37 did not and were suspended. Recommend 37 in all five places.

findings.claim: '1563 - Statute of Artificers: JPs could raise money for poor relief' (also knowledge check 5 and two model answers).
findings.truth: What the lesson describes is the Act for the Relief of the Poor 1563, which made contributions compulsory and allowed imprisonment for refusal. The Statute of Artificers 1563 regulated wages and apprenticeships. Many GCSE textbooks use the wrong label, so this is a teaching-convention call. Recommend renaming to 'Act for the Relief of the Poor' in all four places.

findings.claim: 'her 45-year reign' (L1, L3, L4, L14) and 'Parliament 13 times in 45 years'.
findings.truth: The reign ran from 17 November 1558 to 24 March 1603: 44 years and four months. 45 counts regnal years, so the figure is defensible but a teacher may prefer 44.

findings.claim: 'In 1566, she told Parliament: At present it is not convenient; nor never shall be without some peril unto you and certain danger unto me.'
findings.truth: The wording reads as a genuine Elizabeth quotation, but the year could not be confirmed; it is usually printed as part of her answer to the Commons' petition of 1563. No edit made without confirmation.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Elizabeth I' does not carry this sentence

findings.claim: 'Around 800 rebels were executed' after the Northern Rebellion; 'nearly 5,000 rebels'; 'a royal army of 14,000 men'.
findings.truth: Wikipedia gives about 600 executed (Elizabeth demanded at least 700), about 9,000 rebels and about 22,000 royal troops. GCSE textbooks print the lesson's figures. No single true value found, so no edit.

findings.claim: 'Her Tilbury speech before the Spanish Armada inspired courage and loyalty' (L3, and a model answer in L3).
findings.truth: The Tilbury speech was delivered on 9 August 1588, after Gravelines, while invasion was still feared. Lesson 16 states this correctly. 'Before' is ambiguous rather than flatly wrong, so it is recorded not edited.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Speech to the Troops at Tilbury'; internal L16 statement

findings.claim: After F23, three model answers in Lesson 11 still date Hawkins's slave trading 'from 1564'.
findings.truth: They should read 1562 to match the corrected body text. Left unedited to avoid replacing three long mark-scheme strings for a date already fixed in the lesson body.

findings.claim: glossary_terms carries 'monopoly' twice, at index 0 and index 2, with identical definitions.
findings.truth: The body defines the same term twice. Harmless but untidy; the duplicate flashcard has been replaced.

findings.claim: 'Drake and Hawkins as experienced vice-admirals'; 'Drake once stole GBP 30,000 in a single raid (about GBP 15 million today)'; 'Elizabeth... knighted Drake on his return'.
findings.truth: Drake was Vice-Admiral, Hawkins Rear-Admiral. The GBP 30,000 figure and its modern conversion could not be verified. Drake was knighted on the Golden Hind on 4 April 1581, with a French diplomat performing the act.

findings.claim: Plays 'started at about 3pm'; nobility 'about 60 families... GBP 6,000/year'; gentry 'about 10,000 families... GBP 1,700/year'; L15 'only 60 printing presses', 'around 30 musicians', coronation '10 days of celebrations'.
findings.truth: These are textbook figures that could not be checked against a reference source. Public playhouses are usually said to have opened at 2pm. Recorded, not edited.

findings.claim: The exam tip says students may be asked a 'how convincing' question.
findings.truth: The spec's own table labels the Section B interpretation question 'How far do you agree with this statement?', while live papers use 'How convincing is Interpretation A about...?'. Both describe the same 8-mark AO4 question, so no edit.

findings.claim: Lessons 16 and 17 present the 16-mark historic environment essay without SPaG marks.
findings.truth: Correct. In Paper 2 the 4 SPaG marks sit on the Section A thematic essay (8 + 8 + 4 = 20); Section B's four questions total 40 with the site essay at 16 and no SPaG. The lessons match the spec.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Section A and Section B mark tables; spec p9 (84 marks, 2 hours, 50%)

findings.claim: The lessons assert that the Spanish Armada is the named site for 2027 and Kenilworth Castle for 2028.
findings.truth: Could not be verified: the AQA site-list pages return 404 to WebFetch and this session's WebSearch budget is spent. The claim is left as written; it needs a human check against the board's published list.

summary: 17 lessons checked against the spec and external sources. Five HIGH findings: the examined period given as 1558 rather than c1568; the board named in the two historic environment lessons; a banned band name in an exam tip; William Cecil's death moved from 1598 into 1588-91 in body text, a flashcard and a top-band model answer; and the Northern Rebellion made a consequence of the 1570 papal bull in another model answer. Beneath those, verified corrections to Douai and the Jesuits, the 1571 statutes, Hatton, Cartwright, John Field, Hawkins's first slaving voyage, the magnetic compass, Luther's church door, Essex's age and the gap between his trial and execution. Every lesson except 16 and 17 carried broken auto-generated flashcards: 58 cards rebuilt. Five items need Tom's ruling, chiefly the Old Style / New Style Armada date clash between Lessons 9 and 16.
